cues.text: Section nine: Independent revision questions, written by your tutor.
These are eight practice questions, and each comes with its answer.
Let's work through them in order, and I'll explain the reasoning behind each one so you can answer similar questions on your own.
Question one.
Which CVF culture prioritises stability, procedures and internal control?
The answer is Hierarchy.
CVF stands for the Competing Values Framework, a model that describes organisational culture types.
The Hierarchy culture is the one that values stability, clear procedures and internal control.
If you see those three ideas together, stability, procedures and control, think Hierarchy.
Notice how this links to digital transformation.
A strongly hierarchical culture can make fast, experimental change harder, because its focus is on following established rules.
Question two.
An organisation publicly values experimentation but punishes honest mistakes.
Which Schein level is the deeper obstacle?
The answer is Underlying assumptions.
Schein's model describes culture in levels.
At the surface are visible things, such as artefacts.
Then come espoused values, which are what the organisation says it believes.
At the deepest level are underlying assumptions, the unspoken beliefs people actually act on.
In this question, the organisation says it values experimentation.
That is an espoused value.
But punishing honest mistakes shows what people truly believe, which is that failure is dangerous.
That hidden belief is the underlying assumption, and it is the deeper obstacle, because employees will follow what is rewarded and punished, not what is announced.
Question three.
R&D expenditure is four percent of revenue.
What innovation metric type is this?
The answer is Input.
Research and development spending is a resource put into the innovation effort.
It measures what you invest, not what you produce or achieve.
So four percent of revenue spent on R&D is an input metric.
Question four.
A pilot produced three prototypes but none has delivered benefits yet.
Are these outcomes?
The answer is No, prototypes are outputs.
This is an important distinction.
An output is something produced by an activity, such as a prototype.
An outcome is the benefit or change that results from using it, for example cost savings, better customer experience or higher revenue.
Here, three prototypes exist, but none has delivered benefits yet, so no outcomes have been achieved.
Together with question three, you now have the chain: inputs, such as R&D spending, lead to outputs, such as prototypes, and outputs should lead to outcomes, which are the real benefits.
Question five.
Five of one hundred deployments cause incidents.
What is the change failure rate?
The answer is five percent.
The calculation is simple.
Change failure rate is the number of deployments that cause incidents divided by the total number of deployments.
That is five divided by one hundred, which equals zero point zero five, or five percent.
Question six.
Why use a balanced set of KPIs?
KPI means key performance indicator.
The answer is: a single target can hide trade-offs and encourage gaming.
If you measure only one thing, say speed, people may improve it while quality, cost or customer satisfaction quietly get worse.
That is a trade-off being hidden.
People may also manipulate the single number to look successful, which is gaming.
A balanced set of KPIs lets you see several dimensions at once and reduces that risk.
Question seven.
How does a digital champion help sustain change?
The answer has three parts.
A digital champion supports colleagues, communicates local issues, and reinforces capability.
So the champion helps people around them use new tools and ways of working.
They pass local problems and concerns back to the change leaders, so the issues are heard.
And they help keep skills and confidence strong over time, so the change does not fade after launch.
Question eight.
Why distinguish lead time and cycle time?
The answer is: lead time includes waiting before work; cycle time isolates active workflow elapsed time under the chosen definitions.
So lead time covers the whole period, including the time a request sits waiting before anyone starts on it.
Cycle time looks only at the elapsed time of the active workflow, once work is under way.
Separating them helps you see whether delay comes from waiting or from the work itself.
And note the qualification in the answer: cycle time depends on the chosen definitions, so you must state clearly where the active workflow starts and ends when you measure it.
That completes the eight revision questions for this chapter.
